data.title: Node, NestJS, and RN Async
data.subtitle: nextTick, Nest handler Promises, RN same JS loop

cards.meaning: One JS thread per realm/worker; sync code runs to stack empty; Promise reactions and await resumes are microtasks; setTimeout is a timer-style macrotask; long sync work blocks that JS thread's callbacks. Node/RN add host APIs and extra native threads — they do not replace this model.
cards.notes: Keep the event-loop unit as the primary model; this unit is Node/Nest/RN deltas.

cards.meaning: process.nextTick(fn) schedules fn on Node's nextTick queue, which drains before ordinary Promise microtasks (queueMicrotask / .then). Typical order: sync, nextTick, promise, then timeout.
cards.example:
setTimeout(..., 0); Promise.resolve().then(...); process.nextTick(...); console.log('sync');
// sync, nextTick, promise, timeout (typical)

cards.meaning: Flooding nextTick starves I/O and timers even harder than a Promise microtask flood — the nextTick queue never yields to the rest of the loop. Do not build recursive nextTick pumps.

Know it for interviews and Node/Nest debugging — it is Node-only (not browser or RN JS unless polyfilled). Prefer queueMicrotask or Promises in app code. Historically it runs immediately after this operation, before I/O; it is not your default defer.

Awareness, not memorization-critical: timers (setTimeout/setInterval) → pending callbacks → idle/prepare → poll (I/O) → check (setImmediate) → close. Between phases Node drains nextTick then Promise microtasks. Day-to-day predict-the-output still starts from sync → nextTick → microtasks → macrotasks.
cards.notes: Do not treat phases as more important than microtask vs macrotask.

cards.meaning: Node-specific check-phase deferred callback — macrotask-like, not sync. Not a web standard; RN has no setImmediate. Interview bucket: setImmediate → check phase (Node).
cards.notes: Not a web standard; RN has no setImmediate.

cards.meaning: Both are “soon, not sync.” Relative order can depend on how you entered the loop (timers vs check). Do not memorize fragile ordering puzzles or rely on timeout(0) vs immediate races in production.
cards.notes: Say: both defer to a later macrotask-like turn; setImmediate is Node-specific check-phase.

cards.front: Nest async controller — what gets awaited?
cards.meaning: Nest awaits the handler Promise when you return a Promise or use async. Throw or a rejected Promise on that awaited path goes to exception filters → HTTP error. Signal domain/HTTP errors by throwing on that path.
cards.example: @Get(':id') async findOne(...) { return this.users.findById(id); } // Promise → Nest waits

cards.front: void analytics.track() in Nest handler — risk?
cards.meaning: A fire-and-forget Promise with no catch is an unhandled rejection. Nest only supervises the Promise it awaits. The HTTP response may already be success; a later rejection may log or crash Node depending on flags, and the client will not see it. Supervise with .catch or a job queue.

cards.front: Heavy sync work in Nest async handler?
cards.meaning: async does not move CPU off the event loop. Heavy sync in a handler blocks other requests on that Node process — same single-thread story as a UI freeze, different symptom (latency). Put heavy or slow side work on queues/workers, not as sync CPU or unsupervised Promises on the request thread.

cards.front: Does React Native have a different event loop than the browser?
cards.meaning: No for JS. The JS thread runs Hermes or JSC with the same single-threaded loop, call stack, and micro/macrotask model. Promises, async/await, and setTimeout match browser or Node. Hermes does not change await semantics. What differs is the native side.

Native is multi-threaded; your JS is still one stack per runtime. JS thread: React tree, Promises, timers, most app logic. Native UI threads: views, layout, many platform APIs. Bridge/JSI crosses between them — that does not give JS a different Promise or event-loop model.

cards.front: Large JS work on the RN JS thread?
cards.meaning: A busy JS loop still janks interaction and logic scheduling — same as the web main thread. Native work may run in parallel while JS waits, but your .then still runs on the JS thread when the message comes back.

cards.front: Unhandled rejection: Node vs browser vs RN?
cards.meaning: Browser: silent or noisy failures. Node/Nest: can crash the process depending on flags — know the unhandledRejection policy in production. RN: app instability and noisy logs.

cards.front: React vs Nest on async errors?
cards.meaning: Nest awaits controller Promises. React does not auto-catch async handlers — try/catch or .catch in handlers/effects is your job.

cards.front: Browser vs Node vs RN — thread and timer APIs?
cards.meaning: Single JS thread on all three (tab/worker, isolate/worker_thread, RN JS thread). Extra UI thread: browser compositor, RN native UI; Node HTTP has none. setTimeout exists on all three. process.nextTick and setImmediate are Node-only.
